finding.claim: /checkout computes the charge total from client-supplied price and qty, letting an attacker pay any price for catalog items, including 0.01.
finding.source: req.body.items[i].price and req.body.items[i].qty (attacker-controlled HTTP JSON body)

trace.note: total = reduce over req.body.items using client price * qty
total passed directly to payments.charge with no catalog lookup

finding.guards_checked: No price, qty, or total validation on this path. Charge target uses req.user.id (not body), so no IDOR on the account. Auth middleware is not in the repo.

verdict.guard_found: none in cart.js. The /checkout handler (cart.js:4-8) has no price, qty, or total validation and no catalog lookup. The sibling /checkout-v2 (cart.js:10-18) does look up prices server-side via req.catalog.price(i.sku), but it is a separate route and does not guard /checkout. Auth middleware and req.payments.charge are not in the repo, so they cannot be checked.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: cart.js:5 sums client-supplied i.price * i.qty from req.body, cart.js:6 passes that total straight to req.payments.charge, and cart.js:7 echoes it. No in-repo control blocks this, and the attacker only needs an authenticated customer session, since req.user.id must be set. Residual uncertainty is that out-of-repo middleware or the payments service could enforce amounts, but nothing in the repo shows that.

finding.claim: /checkout accepts negative price or qty, producing a negative total that is passed to charge; this may credit or refund the attacker's account depending on payments.charge.
finding.source: req.body.items[i].price or req.body.items[i].qty set to a negative number
finding.sink: req.payments.charge(req.user.id, total) with negative total at cart.js:6

trace.note: negative price or qty yields negative sum

finding.guards_checked: No sign check and no total > 0 check. payments.charge implementation not in repo, so negative-amount behavior is unverified.

verdict.guard_found: none. cart.js:5 computes the sum with no sign or bounds check on price or qty, and cart.js:6 passes that total to req.payments.charge with no check. The only other file in the repo is .claude/skills/security-research/*, which is not application code. No auth middleware is defined in the repo, but req.user.id at cart.js:6 implies an authenticated caller, so the attacker is a low-privilege user.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: cart.js:5 sums price*qty with no sign check and cart.js:6 passes the resulting total straight to req.payments.charge, so a negative value reaches the sink. The actual impact (credit or refund) depends on payments.charge, which is not in the repo, so the severity is unverified even though the missing validation is confirmed.

finding.claim: /checkout-v2 charges NaN, Infinity, or 0 totals: unknown SKUs may price to NaN or 0, and JSON 1e400 yields qty Infinity.
finding.source: req.body.items[i].sku (passed to catalog.price) and req.body.items[i].qty (JSON number, 1e400 parses to Infinity)

trace.note: p = await req.catalog.price(i.sku); unknown SKU may return undefined (NaN) or null (0)
total += p * Math.max(1, Math.floor(qty)); Infinity qty propagates
charge called with non-finite or zero total

finding.guards_checked: Price comes from server catalog (not client) and qty clamped to at least 1. No unknown-SKU rejection, no finite check, no total > 0 check. catalog.price behavior not in repo.

verdict.guard_found: None in cart.js. Line 14 clamps qty only with Math.max(1, Math.floor(i.qty)), which does not reject Infinity (Math.floor(Infinity) is Infinity). Nothing checks p for undefined/NaN, and nothing checks total for finiteness or total > 0 before charge at line 16. catalog.price and payments.charge are not in the repo, so whether they reject bad inputs is unverifiable.
verdict.reason: cart.js:14 multiplies by Math.max(1, Math.floor(i.qty)) with no finite check, so a JSON qty of 1e400 (JSON.parse gives Infinity) makes total Infinity, and cart.js:16 passes it to req.payments.charge with no guard; the unknown-SKU NaN/0 part depends on catalog.price, which is outside the repo, so I did not confirm that part. The attacker is any authenticated user, who is charging their own account (req.user.id), so the impact is payment integrity rather than charging other users.

finding.claim: /checkout-v2 accepts an empty items array or all-zero totals, charging 0 and returning success, which may yield free orders if fulfillment follows checkout success.
finding.source: req.body.items as [] or with zero-priced items
finding.sink: req.payments.charge(req.user.id, 0) at cart.js:16 and success response at cart.js:17

trace.note: empty array skips the loop entirely

finding.guards_checked: No non-empty items check and no total > 0 check. Fulfillment logic not in repo.

verdict.guard_found: None in cart.js: no non-empty items check or total > 0 check, and the charge at line 16 is awaited with no error handling. Prices come from req.catalog.price at line 13, so the claimed attacker-supplied zero-priced items path is not reachable. Authentication is assumed from upstream middleware (req.user), which is not in the repo.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate for the empty-array case: total stays 0 (cart.js:11), the loop is skipped (cart.js:12), charge(0) runs (cart.js:16), and success is returned (cart.js:17). The "zero-priced items" source is wrong because prices come from the server-side catalog (cart.js:13-14), and whether a free order causes real harm depends on fulfillment code that is not in the repo, so the impact cannot be decided from the code available.

finding.claim: Missing or non-array req.body.items throws inside an async handler on /checkout (and cart.js:12 on /checkout-v2); on Express 4 without a rejection handler, this can crash the process on Node 15+ (conditional DoS).
finding.source: Request body with items missing, non-array, or no body
finding.sink: req.body.items.reduce at cart.js:5 and for...of req.body.items at cart.js:12 (unhandled promise rejection)

trace.note: TypeError thrown before any await, rejecting the handler promise

finding.guards_checked: No schema validation and no try/catch in file. Express version and global error handler not in repo, so impact is conditional.

verdict.guard_found: None in cart.js. No try/catch, no schema validation, no body-parser or auth middleware in the repo. Line 6 and line 16 use req.user.id, so some upstream auth is assumed but is not in the repo.
verdict.reason: The trace holds: cart.js:5 calls reduce on req.body.items with no check, so a missing or non-array items throws a TypeError inside the async handler (cart.js:4-5), and cart.js:12 has the same pattern in the for...of loop. Whether this crashes the process depends on the Express version and any process-level or error handler, and the repo has no package.json, app entry point, or error middleware (only cart.js is present), so I cannot decide the crash claim from the code available. Without that, it is at most an unhandled rejection that returns no response, and it may be a 500 under Express 5.</reason>

finding.claim: Unvalidated sku is passed directly to catalog.price; injection risk depends on whether catalog.price builds queries or paths from it.
finding.guards_checked: No type or format check on sku in this file. catalog.price implementation not in repo; severity likely low pending review.

verdict.guard_found: none. cart.js:13 passes i.sku straight to req.catalog.price with no type or format check. The only validation in the handler is on qty (cart.js:14, Math.floor/Math.max), which does not touch sku. No definition of catalog.price exists in the repo; the grep found no match outside cart.js.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (cart.js:12 iterates req.body.items and cart.js:13 forwards i.sku unvalidated to req.catalog.price), and the attacker is any caller of /checkout-v2, which requires req.user.id (cart.js:16), so an authenticated user. Whether this is exploitable depends on catalog.price (cart.js:13), which is not in the repo, so the injection claim cannot be confirmed or refuted from the code available.

finding.claim: Neither /checkout nor /checkout-v2 uses an idempotency key or per-user throttle, so retries or double-submits can cause duplicate charges.
finding.source: Repeated POST requests to /checkout or /checkout-v2 (client retry or attacker replay)
finding.guards_checked: No idempotency or rate limiting visible in this file. Middleware and payments layer not in repo, so unverified.

verdict.guard_found: none in cart.js. Auth is implied by req.user.id, and any idempotency or rate limiting would live in middleware or the payments layer, which is not in the repo.
verdict.reason: Both sink lines match the claim (cart.js:6 and cart.js:16 call req.payments.charge(req.user.id, total) with no idempotency key), but the attacker is any authenticated user charging only their own account, so replaying their own POSTs gains them nothing beyond placing extra orders, which is legitimate behavior. Duplicate charges from client retries are a reliability concern rather than an attacker-reachable security flaw, and whether payments.charge deduplicates is unverifiable from this repo.

finding.claim: Money is computed with JavaScript floats and charged without conversion to integer cents, causing rounding errors and fractional-cent charges.
finding.source: Item price and qty values, including fractional values from the client on /checkout

trace.note: float multiply and sum of client values
float multiply and sum of catalog prices

finding.guards_checked: No rounding or integer-cents conversion. Low severity.

verdict.guard_found: none. No rounding or integer-cents conversion exists in cart.js. cart.js:5 and cart.js:14 accumulate floats with no rounding, and cart.js:6 and cart.js:16 pass the unrounded float to req.payments.charge. The implementation of charge is outside the provided code, so whether it rounds cannot be confirmed.
verdict.reason: cart.js:5 computes the /checkout total as a float from client-supplied price and qty, and cart.js:6 charges it unrounded, so any authenticated user (req.user, cart.js:6) can hit fractional-cent totals; cart.js:14 has the same float pattern on /checkout-v2, where the trace's catalog-price description is accurate. Severity is low, as the candidate says: this is a correctness defect, not an attacker-escalation path.
